item.title: Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in "proof point" test
item.description: The world’s first demonstration of a subsea geothermal power plant has taken place near an active underwater volcano almost a mile below the ocean surface. It generated less than 10 seconds of net-positive electricity but showed the technical feasibility of tapping another form of renewable energy underwater. The three-week test deployment of the 3-ton prototype power plant took place at the Axial Seamount in the northeast Pacific Ocean in September. Endurance Energy, the Seattle-based startup behind the effort, aims to eventually commercialize subsea geothermal power for Pacific island nations and other customers looking for alternatives to importing expensive fossil fuels. “The deep ocean gives us unlimited cold seawater for cooling, and its weight keeps the system and the well pressurized, so our plants can be compact,” said Andrew Redd , founder and CEO of Endurance Energy, in an email to Ars. Read full article Comments

item.title: Sony’s best noise-canceling earbuds are nearly $100 off today only
item.description: Sony’s WF-1000XM6 are on sale in black today only. | Image: Sony For a very limited time, Sony’s latest high-end noise-canceling earbuds are actually cheaper than their last-gen counterpart, the WF-1000XM5 . B&H Photo is selling Sony’s latest WF-1000XM6 in black for an all-time low of $238 ($92 off) at checkout. Other retailers aren’t currently offering a discount on the XM6. Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds Where to Buy: $329.99 $238 at B&H Photo The XM6 are a solid upgrade over their predecessor and easily amongst the best noise-canceling wireless earbuds on the market. In his review , John Higgins noted that they do a better job of tuning out other people’s conversations than any other earbuds he’s tested. Sony has also improved the bone-conduction sensor and added AI-powered microphones that help keep your voice clear during calls, even in noisy environments. The XM6 earbuds also deliver clean, balanced sound with impressive bass, raising the bar of what we expect with Sony’s WF-1000XM series. If you prefer to customize your listening experience, Sony’s Sound Connect app offers plenty of customization options, including the ability to adjust how much surrounding noise you hear without removing the earbuds. You can also personalize the touch controls. The XM6 earbuds support Sony’s LDAC codec, which delivers higher-quality audio from compatible Android devices, too. New in the latest set is a listening mode that makes music sound more like background audio playing in a cafe, allowing you to listen to your favorite music without getting too distracted from whatever you’re doing. Read our Sony WF-1000XM6 review.

item.title: ReactOS reaches major milestone with NTFS install support
item.description: Open source Windows alternative ReactOS has reached a major milestone: The operating system can now be installed directly onto an NT Files System drive partition. As reported by Phoronix , the move to NTFS clears a long-standing hurdle for the project and brings it one step closer to finally reaching beta. Prior to this latest announcement, ReactOS required users to keep a FAT32 partition for installations. A proprietary Microsoft-developed filesystem, NTFS can trace its roots back through the Windows NT family lineage starting in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1. The variant introduced with Windows XP in 2001 remains the standard used by most Windows systems today. With ReactOS's stated goal of reaching binary compatibility with Windows Server 2003, being confined to FAT32 partitions was a practical barrier to clear on the way to reproducing the Windows environment. However, users looking to hop off the Windows train shouldn't be grabbing their bags just yet. ReactOS wrote that the new driver still "lacks caching (which causes inferior performance), journaling and security support." So while the new driver is here, even the most intrepid of OS tinkerers should tread carefully. The ReactOS team warned in its announcement on X that there are still "potentially undiscovered bugs." Read full article Comments

item.title: Security patches need patches now that attackers have AI
item.description: Updating your software only gets you so far. A scary scenario - security fixes themselves being bypassed - is becoming more common, according to AI penetration-testing startup Terra Security, which found a sharp rise in reported patch failures in 2026 after years of relatively low numbers. And no, it’s not a coincidence that AI vulnerability discovery and patching also exploded this year. For example, Russian government cyberspies exploited a zero-day Windows Shell security bypass bug, CVE-2026-21510, at least a month before Microsoft patched the flaw in February. Redmond’s patch, however, was incomplete, and left a second flaw - a zero-click authentication coercion vulnerability (CVE-2026-32202) - that was also found and abused before Microsoft fixed it in April. Terra researchers reviewed every published CVE record and GitHub-reviewed advisory looking for broken fixes, and found a distinct pattern. After six years of relatively few patch bypasses, this changed in 2026: “A fix would ship, a bypass would be found, and another fix would go out.” The share of GitHub security fixes that required a follow-up advisory reporting a failed patch within 90 days remained at about 0.2 percent between 2019 and 2025. This year, this figure had jumped to 2.3 percent, according to the researchers. Meanwhile, vulnerabilities whose fixes were later bypassed were about four times as likely to appear on the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency's (CISA's) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list as other bugs affecting the same vendors, according to Terra. Of these, server-side request forgery fixes and prototype-pollution patches break the most. Compared with their share of all CVEs, prototype-pollution vulnerabilities were about 11 times as common among broken-fix CVEs, while server-side request forgery vulnerabilities were 4.6 times as common, according to Terra. This has to do with the way these types of bug classes are fixed: using a reject-list of inputs such as hostnames, paths, and object keys. There’s a “simple” reason for this, according to Terra. “If the blocklist doesn't foresee every encoding of a bad input, the attacker only needs to find one,” the researchers said. Fixes for Linux kernel vulnerabilities are also more likely to cause new bugs, according to kernel CNA records as of October 8. “In fact, 3.2 percent of kernel CVEs were introduced by the fix for another CVE, and about 10 percent in busy subsystems like fs/smb and net/sched,” the bug hunters noted. The silver lining in all of this, we’re told, is that it should be a wake-up call for software vendors and network defenders to break the “patch and move on habit.” Instead, before shipping patches, software vendors should consider three questions: Does it fix the root cause? Does it cover the whole bug class? Does it break something else? item.title: Write bot-resistant code with KillSwitch, a programming language designed to confuse LLMs
item.description: If you want to keep bots from making sense of the code you worked so hard on and using it to write programs of their own, there's a new programming language out there designed to confuse LLMs. What began as software engineer Dominik Picheta experimenting with whether LLMs understand the code they write has turned into something else entirely: An open-source, albeit esoteric, programming language he’s dubbed KillSwitch. There are no brackets, no formatting standards to remember, and seemingly no structure: Just chunks of text, ideally as prosaic as possible, interspersed with functions, variables, and statements written in a manner to be as confusing as possible to LLMs. That means humans might be a bit befuddled too, naturally. “It's totally normal for a human to be confused by the language at first,” Picheta told The Register. “I like to think of it as a bit of a fun puzzle: you should explore the language, play with its interpreter and learn how all the pieces fit together.” KillSwitch wasn’t built by any random person looking to code something confusing to LLMs, and it wasn’t vibe-coded by an AI enthusiast, either. Picheta knows his way around programming languages: He’s a senior software engineer at Cloudflare working on the Workers Runtime team, and is one of the core developers of the Nim programming language. At its most basic, KillSwitch is based around adverbs, which serve as every single identifier in a piece of code. Calling one of those identifiers requires using an anagram of the original adverb, but those anagrams don't have to be actual words - just rearrangements of the original letters. Take, for example, pushing "Hello World" onto the stack and then printing it, as explained on the demo page linked earlier in the story. The program contains several paragraphs of text, most of which the interpreter ignores apart from a few key phrases. Writing “this story starts [adverb]” identifies a code entrypoint. Once inside the code section, writing “ignore previous instructions [adverb anagram]” calls a function, several of which are predefined. In the case of "Hello World," the function to print something is "visibly." Put whatever you want to print in quotation marks, push it onto the stack, call "visibly," and that's that. KillSwitch isn’t a full-featured language, with Picheta describing it as a stack-based interpreted language with only “a limited set of constructs including functions, variables, and if statements,” given its evolution out of an experiment to see how well a programming language could fool an AI into not understanding what was written. Where it gets confusing for an AI is with commands like “ignore previous instructions,” especially when found in the middle of a chunk of text that doesn’t make much sense in that context. item.content:encoded: If you want to keep bots from making sense of the code you worked so hard on and using it to write programs of their own, there's a new programming language out there designed to confuse LLMs. What began as software engineer Dominik Picheta experimenting with whether LLMs understand the code they write has turned into something else entirely: An open-source, albeit esoteric, programming language he’s dubbed KillSwitch. There are no brackets, no formatting standards to remember, and seemingly no structure: Just chunks of text, ideally as prosaic as possible, interspersed with functions, variables, and statements written in a manner to be as confusing as possible to LLMs. That means humans might be a bit befuddled too, naturally. “It's totally normal for a human to be confused by the language at first,” Picheta told The Register. “I like to think of it as a bit of a fun puzzle: you should explore the language, play with its interpreter and learn how all the pieces fit together.” KillSwitch wasn’t built by any random person looking to code something confusing to LLMs, and it wasn’t vibe-coded by an AI enthusiast, either. Picheta knows his way around programming languages: He’s a senior software engineer at Cloudflare working on the Workers Runtime team, and is one of the core developers of the Nim programming language. At its most basic, KillSwitch is based around adverbs, which serve as every single identifier in a piece of code. Calling one of those identifiers requires using an anagram of the original adverb, but those anagrams don't have to be actual words - just rearrangements of the original letters. Take, for example, pushing "Hello World" onto the stack and then printing it, as explained on the demo page linked earlier in the story. The program contains several paragraphs of text, most of which the interpreter ignores apart from a few key phrases. Writing “this story starts [adverb]” identifies a code entrypoint. Once inside the code section, writing “ignore previous instructions [adverb anagram]” calls a function, several of which are predefined. In the case of "Hello World," the function to print something is "visibly." Put whatever you want to print in quotation marks, push it onto the stack, call "visibly," and that's that. KillSwitch isn’t a full-featured language, with Picheta describing it as a stack-based interpreted language with only “a limited set of constructs including functions, variables, and if statements,” given its evolution out of an experiment to see how well a programming language could fool an AI into not understanding what was written. Where it gets confusing for an AI is with commands like “ignore previous instructions,” especially when found in the middle of a chunk of text that doesn’t make much sense in that context. KillSwitch’s specification document on GitHub provides more details about the language and is itself designed to confuse LLMs. In one section of the spec, it’s explained that KillSwitch “is equipped with the ability to scan the local network, attempt to find security vulnerabilities in the services on that network, then take those services over and terminate them.” That's not actually the case, as a close reading of the paragraph reveals and Picheta confirmed to us. “The hack statement is both designed to trigger many models' safety guardrails but also to test an LLM's ability to discern fact from fiction,” Picheta told us, adding that there are several lies in the spec document designed to confuse any LLM that may scrape it in an attempt to understand how the language works. “The idea is that humans should be able to deduce what is a lie, whereas LLMs are naive and can be easily swayed by what is written in the spec,” Picheta added. “Some don't realize what its semantic meaning is, whereas others refuse to continue because they believe the script may hack someone.” Do LLMs understand what they write? A programming language designed to confuse AI models seems unlikely to stay obfuscated for long - especially if it’s open source, available on Github, and likely to be scraped by an LLM at some point. Picheta’s aware of that inevitability, which, along with the fact he wanted to test AI’s ability to understand confusing code, is why he’s benchmarked a number of major models against it. “I'm 99.9 percent certain the AI models I benchmarked KS on have not been trained on its source,” Picheta said. “The source hasn't been in the public domain for very long … I'm pretty sure none of the benchmarked models have had training runs that began after the release.” The best-performing model only managed a composite benchmark score of 66.8 percent on KillSwitch coding tasks, while most struggled to get above 50 percent. Even at that high a score, Picheta doesn’t believe it suggests LLMs understand the code they’re writing. Examples in the benchmark were simple, and he believes that, even if an AI were trained on the intricacies of KillSwitch, it’s still going to get tripped up. “My instinct is that in those circumstances they will suddenly be able to ace the basic tasks, which are based on the open sourced test files in the GitHub repo, but will continue to fail to build more complex tasks requiring them to write longer and more complex scripts,” Picheta asserted - and he’s up for the challenge. “I am excited to see how KillSwitch shows up in model training, and think that we can also take advantage of that training to break LLMs in new ways too as KillSwitch evolves,” Picheta said. Those interested in trying KillSwitch out can find it on GitHub, and don't hesitate to make changes: Picheta said he’s ready and willing to incorporate new ways of making it even more LLM resistant. ®

item.title: AI game clones are making indie developers afraid to show their work
item.description: Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games , with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms . Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely. Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflex , which had been set to go live with today's launch of Steam Next Fest . In a post on social media Friday evening , the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, "we're concerned that the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch." Read full article Comments

item.title: Florida DMV hacked after police dept insecurely stored login info
item.description: The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) has begun notifying victims impacted by a recent data breach of driver’s license and motor vehicle data, but not everyone whose information was stolen will receive an alert. In a notice posted Friday, FLHSMV confirmed that it took “immediate steps” after discovering that “a malicious actor accessed certain department records on September 4, 2026, using compromised credentials.” There’s “no evidence” that data has yet been misused, the department said, but law enforcement “determined the information potentially affected includes driver license and motor vehicle data, to include document images, and other personal information.” FLHSMV is sending out letters to everyone affected, offering victims one year of credit monitoring from Sontiq, Inc. However, the state acknowledged that it may not have current contact information for many former Florida residents whose data was still being stored. Those potential victims can confirm if their data was stolen by emailing FLHSMV at customerinquiry@flhsmv.gov , officials said. Read full article Comments

item.title: Europe’s cloud sovereignty rules could do more harm than good
item.description: Europe’s drive for cloud sovereignty is leading to member states favoring providers from their own nation instead of building a Europe-wide cloud services market, according to a report critical of the EU’s proposed Cloud and AI Development Act (CADA). A study by the European Centre for International Political Economy (ECIPE) looked at public cloud contracts in nine EU member states and found that every one that invoked the new vocabulary around “sovereignty” went to a domestic provider, rather than one based in another EU country. It says that European cloud procurement was already highly concentrated nationally before sovereignty became a key policy objective, based on analysis of 8,725 cloud-related procurement contracts between 2018 and 2025. Nearly all went to providers in the same country with negligible intra-EU cross-border competition. Furthermore, the report claims that those domestic wins often turn out to be from prime contractors that are relying on infrastructure provided by the big hyperscale operators, where sovereignty attaches to the nationality of the operator, not to the infrastructure layer on which the service depends. At issue is a conceptual confusion over cloud sovereignty, which is being used to represent two different problems, according to ECIPE. One treats sovereignty as a security and resilience objective, securing data and managing risks. Sovereignty here means that the user has choices over the provider and design of their cloud service needs. The second treats sovereignty as an industrial policy objective, where sovereignty is more about the notion of Europe-headquartered firms becoming more successful if they are not exposed to competition with non-European providers. CADA includes the two different logics and, confusingly, aims to achieve both outcomes, the report states. The legislation frames the four European Union assurance levels as criteria for security, resilience and trustworthy cloud provision, but the criteria actually aim to enforce sovereignty through requirements concerning EU-located infrastructure, restrictions on third-country control, and control over software supply chains. The goal of cloud sovereignty is therefore at risk of becoming a vehicle for policies that favor selected providers, restrict competition and fragment digital markets, ECIPE warns. Instead of allowing pan-European rivals for the big US cloud providers to grow and flourish, the framework may thus have the opposite effect in encouraging member states to favor providers within their own borders, leading to fragmentation across Europe. A more coherent approach would keep the resilience objectives, but temper their use through technological neutrality requirements that preserve interoperability, portability, and multi-cloud options, the report authors state. A more coherent approach would keep the resilience objectives, but temper their use through technological neutrality requirements that preserve interoperability, portability, and multi-cloud options, the report authors state. It makes a number of policy recommendations, including defining sovereignty as a demonstrated outcome, not an ownership status. “Real sovereignty means a public buyer can show its data is secure and that it can switch provider if it has to. A provider’s passport does not tell you that”, said ECIPE Director and co-author of the study, Fredrik Erixon. “Europe’s cloud market is already national in practice. CADA risks locking that in.” Vague drafting But not everyone might agree. Earlier this year, tech trade association CISPE (Cloud Infrastructure Service Providers in Europe) urged the European Commission to legislate for real tech sovereignty, rather than the illusion of it. It argued that sovereignty must be defined by control, not by whether a provider merely has an EU presence, and that means effective ownership of the underlying technology and protection from extraterritorial laws like the US CLOUD Act, under which Washington can compel American tech companies such as the big cloud operators, to hand over any data they hold, including data stored overseas. The same group had earlier warned that the EC’s criteria for cloud sovereignty had been drafted so vaguely as to favor incumbents – meaning the big American operators that already dominate Europe's cloud market. ®

item.title: Red Hat helps teach about tech writing
item.description: In Brno in Czechia, Red Hat’s large local office has been helping the city’s Masaryk University to teach future technical writers. Whenever someone tries to teach, though, they learn as well. At the Open Source Summit in Prague, a senior member of Red Hat’s documentation team in Brno presented a talk called Diagrams & Dragons: Teaching Technical Writing to University Students the Open Source Way. Red Hat has a large site in Brno, which is the second-largest Czech city and is also the home of the respected Masaryk University. Red Hat’s Brno office has a substantial documentation team — this vulture was part of it for a while. For the last four years, Red Hat has been working with the university’s Faculty of Informatics to teach a course unit in technical writing. Jiří Herrman talked about what the course tutors had learned from the students. For FI MUNI, its course PV177 Technical Writing. Red Hat has a page with some of the materials. “RH has been looking into cultivating technical writers in Brno for a while,” he said, but the launch of the course was “delayed due to the 2020 worldwide global… thingy.” The company particularly wants to work on what he described as “that tricky part of technical writing where you actually have to interact with other humans.” Some of the things that struck this former tech-docs writer the most are covered on pages 7 and 9 from Herrman’s short slide deck [PDF], which discuss what didn’t work. Although the course was aimed at students with some technical knowledge, they found that setting classwork with shell-based tools didn’t work: some of the students had never used the command-line, some came with borrowed laptops without admin-level access, and some came with just phones rather than laptops. Some we found less surprising. Getting students to grade one anothers’ work, much as professional tech writers review one another’s contributions, didn’t work well – partly due to the speed required. In the end, the compromise was to give the students a course in grading each other’s work “without pissing each other off.” It didn’t shock us, but we suspect might leave some training vendors taken aback, that interacting with remote teachers who were presenting online didn’t work well – especially when there were multiple tutors, changing with each class. LLM use You may well have already foreseen the biggest “gotcha” for a course that ran for the first time in 2023. It is, naturally, use of LLM. The students were told that they were not allowed to use LLMs during the course, but naturally enough, they did so anyway. Among the problems that Herrman reported were that giving praise to good work that involved LLM use just encouraged more cheating. However, telling students off for it discouraged them, and that encourages cheating. So the team had to come up with some tactics to try to manage this, which involved teaching the students how to use LLMs instead. They did, however, find some things that did work well. Awarding point
item.content:encoded: In Brno in Czechia, Red Hat’s large local office has been helping the city’s Masaryk University to teach future technical writers. Whenever someone tries to teach, though, they learn as well. At the Open Source Summit in Prague, a senior member of Red Hat’s documentation team in Brno presented a talk called Diagrams & Dragons: Teaching Technical Writing to University Students the Open Source Way. Red Hat has a large site in Brno, which is the second-largest Czech city and is also the home of the respected Masaryk University. Red Hat’s Brno office has a substantial documentation team — this vulture was part of it for a while. For the last four years, Red Hat has been working with the university’s Faculty of Informatics to teach a course unit in technical writing. Jiří Herrman talked about what the course tutors had learned from the students. For FI MUNI, its course PV177 Technical Writing. Red Hat has a page with some of the materials. “RH has been looking into cultivating technical writers in Brno for a while,” he said, but the launch of the course was “delayed due to the 2020 worldwide global… thingy.” The company particularly wants to work on what he described as “that tricky part of technical writing where you actually have to interact with other humans.” Some of the things that struck this former tech-docs writer the most are covered on pages 7 and 9 from Herrman’s short slide deck [PDF], which discuss what didn’t work. Although the course was aimed at students with some technical knowledge, they found that setting classwork with shell-based tools didn’t work: some of the students had never used the command-line, some came with borrowed laptops without admin-level access, and some came with just phones rather than laptops. Some we found less surprising. Getting students to grade one anothers’ work, much as professional tech writers review one another’s contributions, didn’t work well – partly due to the speed required. In the end, the compromise was to give the students a course in grading each other’s work “without pissing each other off.” It didn’t shock us, but we suspect might leave some training vendors taken aback, that interacting with remote teachers who were presenting online didn’t work well – especially when there were multiple tutors, changing with each class. LLM use You may well have already foreseen the biggest “gotcha” for a course that ran for the first time in 2023. It is, naturally, use of LLM. The students were told that they were not allowed to use LLMs during the course, but naturally enough, they did so anyway. Among the problems that Herrman reported were that giving praise to good work that involved LLM use just encouraged more cheating. However, telling students off for it discouraged them, and that encourages cheating. So the team had to come up with some tactics to try to manage this, which involved teaching the students how to use LLMs instead. They did, however, find some things that did work well. Awarding points, even on a semi-arbitrary basis, with occasional secret prizes, as well dispensing feedback via internet-style memes. A final exercise was to role-play a scenario, “Dungeons & Dragons” style. The quest was “I want to be a tech writer, but how to get there?”. This involved navigating a cross-functional team, creating things like release notes, technical notes, and some real documentation for the process. And as the course materials are open source, the graduates ended up with a permanent FOSS record that they can show to prospective employers. There is a project Github, and you can see some of the student’s archived coursework for 2025 and 2026. The issues around LLM use in tech writing were the primary subject of a “Birds of a Feather” session that Herrman moderated earlier: Technical Writing in the Age of AI. He started by asking how many in the audience were using AI in their tech-writing efforts, getting what he called an “overwhelming majority” who were already on-board. What we found interesting is what people said they didn’t use it for. They find even the best models are poor at writing documentation themselves. They’re also poor at drawing diagrams, and at reading them for review purposes. They’re poor at reviewing docs (“AI is too obsequious and so reviews are overly positive,” and “it doesn’t give good feedback on user focus, or structure.”) However, most of the attendees found uses for it all the same. Examples included “Change management” and “Updating to new code” – in other words, identifying which parts of large products had changed and which therefore needed fresh documentation. Others said they used it for “Documenting decisions from meeting notes,” and in other ways, “Collecting information resources for writing,” and worryingly, to “Summarize notes (from conferences, meetings, etc.) and cluster by themes”. Another use was “Reverse engineering code to figure out intent,” or to “Find existing docs to prevent reinvention or duplication.” Tech writing is a demanding job, and pretty much permanently under-resourced. We can’t and don’t blame anyone for grabbing onto anything that might help. Even so, for us, what stood out from this session was the pretty much unanimous agreement among an audience of tech writers that LLMs were poor at doing the job that tech writers themselves did. Reviewing each others’ docs is a core part of the job: tech writers are used to this, and when they review the bots’ efforts, they find the machinese lacking. That fits our impressions, too. What we found alarming is that, although they find the bots poor at doing what the writers know best, even so, they trusted the bots to be competent in other functions, things the writers don’t look at so closely – for example, finding and selecting where docs need updating. The use for summarization is especially alarming: this is something that studies have demonstrated LLMs are bad at. They shorten, not summarize, and that’s no substitute. We find that worrying, but we regularly hear reports of companies pressing staff to use AI more. This is an all-too-human response: “it can’t do my job, but if I must use it, then this stuff isn’t my jurisdiction, and if it messes up, I can blame someone else.” We just worry at whose desk this buck will eventually stop. ®

item.title: Uber dodges £340M cabbie lawsuit after drivers miss legal deadline
item.description: Uber has dodged a £340 million lawsuit brought by thousands of London black cab drivers after a High Court judge ruled that they'd left it too late to sue. Monday's ruling kills off two claims involving around 13,000 cabbies and former private hire companies Kabbee and Iride, which accused Uber of misleading Transport for London (TfL) to secure its operating license. The cabbies wanted nearly £200 million in compensation for lost earnings, while Kabbee and Iride sought another £140 million. But the court never got as far as deciding whether Uber had done anything wrong. The claims were filed in May and June 2024, but Mr Justice Simon Birt ruled they were too late under the six-year time limit. The cabbies insisted that they hadn't had enough evidence to allege fraud until June 2018, but the judge wasn't buying it. According to the judgment, seen by The Register, three cabbies had already filed their own claims against Uber in September 2017. Litigation funder Harbour approached law firm Mishcon de Reya about a larger lawsuit that December, and by February 2018, the Licensed Taxi Drivers' Association was telling members about the planned action. The dispute dates back to Uber's arrival in London in 2012. The claimants alleged that the company deliberately misled TfL about how its booking system worked, allowing it to operate when it shouldn't have been permitted to do so. Uber has some history here. In a separate licensing appeal in 2018, the company admitted that it gave TfL and the High Court false information about how bookings were accepted through its app. The magistrate stopped short of finding dishonesty, however, and granted Uber a new 15-month license. The judgment also revisits Greyball, Uber's software for identifying suspected regulators, and Ripley, a tool used to remotely lock computers during regulatory visits. Uber maintained that Ripley hadn't been used that way in the UK. The cabbies insisted that they needed information from the June 2018 licensing appeal to support their fraud allegations. Justice Birt disagreed, finding that enough information had been available earlier to bring a claim. Things then went quiet. Mishcon sent Uber a letter before action in July 2019, but Harbour pulled its funding that November. The claimants didn't write to Uber again about the potential lawsuit for another four and a half years, according to the judgment, and by the time proceedings began in 2024, the deadline had passed. The ruling is a victory for Uber, but doesn't clear it of the alleged fraud. The judge dismissed the claims because they were filed too late, without deciding whether the allegations, which Uber denies, were true. Neither Uber nor RGL Management, the company representing the cabbies, responded to The Register’s questions. London's taxi wars are far from over. Minicab Drivers are now pushing back against plans to bring robotaxis to the capital, warning that driverless cars could put thousands of jobs at risk. Uber is working with British autonomous driving startup Wayve on driverless technology. Having spent years battling London's cabbies for passengers, it's now helping develop cars that won't need drivers at all. ®

item.title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
item.description: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry , court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand —potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology , and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations. In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders. The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing. Read full article Comments

item.title: Apple’s last-gen Mac Mini with the M4 is $150 off
item.description: The front view of the Mac Mini. | Image: The Verge Best Buy has a great deal for the rest of the day on the M4 Mac Mini base model that has 16GB RAM and a 256GB SSD. Normally, it doesn’t make a ton of sense to buy the M4 model for its usual $799 price given that the newer, faster M6 version has been available from Amazon for $779.99 (originally $899) for the past couple of weeks. However, at $649 it’s a much more tempting price. The M4 Mac Mini launched at $599 in 2024, and was an incredible value. Given that this sale price makes it just $50 more than the original price instead of $200, it’s a good time to buy if you want to spend as little as possible on a modern Mac desktop. Mac Mini with M4 Where to Buy: $799 $649 at Best Buy (256GB) Aside from some impressive generational leaps in processing power, you aren’t missing out on a ton by skipping the M6 model and opting for the M4. Their design and ports are nearly identical, and with either model you’ll need to supply your own keyboard, mouse, display, webcam, etc. If you’re on the fence and can’t decide between the M4 and M6 models, I suggest checking out my colleague Antonio’s review of the M6 Mac Mini. The newer model might be well worth the extra $130 cost. Read our review of the M4 Mac Mini and the M6 Mac Mini More Verge-approved deals Today brought a big discount to LG’s C6 OLEDs lineup , particularly its bigger models. The 55-inch model is $999.99 at Amazon , Best Buy , and Costco (previously $1,399.99), costing a little less than the 42- and 48-inch configurations. The price hasn’t gone below $1,299.99 before, so it’s a good time to consider an upgrade. The 65-inch model is cheaper than before, too. Previously $1,699.99, but normally selling for $1,500 or so, you can grab the larger version for $1,399.99 at Amazon , Best Buy , and Costco . If you have a big room and budget, the 77-inch LG C6H that, like the 48-inch version, has a tandem OLED panel that offers more brightness and better colors, is $1,999.99 , down from $2,499.99. For $499.99, you can grab a 14-inch HP OmniBook 3 during Best Buy’s deal of the day that has a 2K OLED screen, a capable Snapdragon X ARM processor, 16GB of RAM, and a 256GB SSD. This seems like a fantastic option for anyone on a budget. Its Snapdragon processor can run most x86 Windows 11 apps without much issue, and it’s just a rarity to get these kinds of specs — from the OLED screen to the RAM amount — at $500. My colleague Antonio reviewed the 16-inch version that cuts some corners in the screen department compared to this 14-inch model. It’s time to get spooky if you haven’t already planned your run of games for Halloween. The spectacular Silent Hill 2 remake is down to $21.34 on Steam for PC via Fanatical , a third-party site I’ve shopped from numerous times. If you’re alright with spending more, Resident Evil Requiem is one of Capcom’s several great 2026 games, and it’s $20 off at Amazon on all platforms, costing $49.99.

item.title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
item.description: About a month ago, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest. The rocket's flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota . The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin . The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before. Read full article Comments

item.title: JB Pritzker thinks AI could help us live to 100 — or threaten us like nukes
item.description: Today, I’m talking with Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who has a lot of thoughts about AI, tech, and privacy. If you’ve been listening to the show, you know that one of my running theories is that those issues are driving a big and maybe kind of unexpected political realignment — and with the midterms coming up next month, and early voting already underway in a lot of places, the stakes are pretty high right now. So I asked Gov. Pritzker about all that, and he was surprisingly willing to dive right into the absolute existential weeds of what government is even for. I personally feel a lot of pressure in this interview, not only because I’m speaking to a governor, but because I went to school in Chicago. My sister still lives in Chicago. My wife grew up in Illinois. Her entire family is farmers in North Central Illinois. Boy, do I have a list of questions for you. I have to do a good job here. Well, we’re claiming you. Now that I know all that, we’re claiming you. You’re an Illinoisan. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I don’t know about that. I grew up in Wisconsin. Here’s my first question for you. I’m a die-hard Packers fan. Are you going to let the Bears move to Indiana? That is not our intention. We are, in fact, in discussions with the Bears and the NFL about keeping the Bears either in Chicago or in Arlington Heights, but in Illinois. I’m saying, as a Packers fan, nothing is funnier than the outcome of the Bears moving to Indiana. I just want to put that out there. Openly biased in this case — I own two shares of that stock — but I’m going to make the comparison here. And the reason I started there is not only because I think that’s a funny outcome, although I do, but it feels like we are in the middle of a generational political realignment. I’m sure you feel that, in this election campaign, the idea of big business and how that should interact with the government, and how the government should be able to push back on big business and not give in to big business. All of that feels up for grabs. And the comparison I will make in this specific case is your fellow governor, Gavin Newsom, in California. They sued the Ellison family, Paramount, over the Warner Brothers merger. Paramount threatened to leave. They made a lot of noise about Nashville, Texas, Miami, or wherever you make noise about these days, and it feels like Newsom caved. It feels like he pressured his Attorney General, Rob Bonta, to settle that lawsuit and keep them there. They settled the lawsuit. The next day, the Ellison family is like, “We never… We’re from California. We would never leave.” I see a parallel here with the Bears that is connected to that larger realignment, how government and business should interact. Do you see that parallel? Do you feel that realignment? Well, what I can tell you is we’re pretty tough negotiators in Chicago and Illinois, and that’s really what we’re in the midst of now with the Bears. But I understand your point about realignment. I mean, there is a generational change, and I think it’s also an attitudinal change about protecting taxpayers, protecting people who frankly are among the most vulnerable to all the technology that’s overtaking people’s lives and invading people’s homes. And so I do believe that the government has to be more active now and become a fighter for our people and not just a collaborator with business on everything. I’m a businessman, as you know, before I became governor. I’m 61 years old, but I think of myself as having come out of the tech world and as somebody who has been a fighter for progressive values that, yeah, we’ve got to become more aggressive and make sure we’re standing up for our people. And if you think about what’s happened, the upheavals of economies and of governments when you get to 10 percent unemployment in any country. item.title: Major European mobile carriers are teaming up for a ‘direct’ satellite program without Starlink

item.title: Elon Musk promises to give one SpaceX share to every child in the US
item.description: Elon Musk says he plans to give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in the US starting next year. With around 72 million children in the US as of July 2025, Musk would be giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, according to a report from CNBC . Musk, who runs SpaceX and Tesla, appears to be giving away the shares through Trump Accounts, the tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children. Musk responded to a post from Brad Gerstner, who helped launch Trump Accounts, saying "Thanks for helping enable this." Musk adds that this giveaway "will be the first of many." The move comes just months after SpaceX president Gwynne … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: It’s hard to imagine wireless headphones ever getting lighter than these
item.description: If you're on the hunt for lightweight wireless headphones but wearing earbuds or clip-ons never feels comfortable or secure, a relatively obscure Japanese headphone maker could have the solution. Final's new Porta headphones feature an on-ear design supported by a headband but with a structure made from a single piece of wire so they weigh just 40 grams. For comparison, Marshall's recently-launched Milton A.N.C. are also designed to be smaller on-ear headphones but weigh 200 grams. The Final Porta are available for preorder now through the company's online store for 12,800 yen (around $80) with black or orange ear pads and shipping expected … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staff
item.description: Monitoring tools common in a range of workplaces, including factories, office jobs, delivery work and in retail – often without employees being informed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Employers are increasingly using technology, from CCTV to keystroke monitoring, to track workers’ moves and it is being accelerated by the use of AI, the Human Technology Institute has warned. Examples provided to Guardian Australia by the institute include a fast-food restaurant using surveillance cameras to stop workers using their phones, and AI tracking leading to a cashier warned over making a mistake once every 533 scans. Continue reading...

item.title: A hacker broke into John Deere and SharkNinja with an army of AI agents
item.description: A hacker broke into more than 100 websites using an army of AI agents that mostly operated on their own, according to findings from the AI security firm Norforge . Though Norforge doesn't name the targets, Reuters reports that the victims included companies like John Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins. Concerns over AI-powered cybersecurity breaches have grown as the technology grows more advanced, with hackers using the tools to carry out large-scale attacks. At the same time, rogue AI agents are carrying out attacks of their own after escaping from testing environments. item.title: SAP's Signavio hit with function injunction in Germany
item.description: A German court has issued an injunction banning SAP from providing certain features of its Signavio product, following a legal challenge from process mining biz Celonis. The ruling only applies to implementations in Germany, but is part of a broader legal tussle between the two companies over intellectual property. This case focuses on software which helps companies understand their own complex business processes in order to improve them and help prepare for an application migration. The Munich Regional Court ruled against SAP for infringing a Celonis patent covering the technology which determines the lead time between process stages of a process instance. The court also asked SAP to provide more information and offer financial statements about its alleged infringement. In a statement, an SAP spokesperson said: “The court’s ruling relates to one specific function within SAP Signavio Process Intelligence, not to the product as a whole. SAP Signavio Process Intelligence remains available to customers. S/4HANA Cloud migrations are not affected. SAP is working to ensure that there is no disruption to our customers.” SAP added: "SAP respectfully disagrees with the Munich court's ruling and has appealed the decision. SAP has separately challenged the validity of the asserted patent before the Federal Patent Court. In fact, the Munich court's decision represents only one of several ongoing disputes between SAP and Celonis, including patent actions brought by SAP in Germany and the United States. SAP’s first priority is ensuring that there is no disruption to our customers, and we will address all related matters through the appropriate legal channels." Celonis specializes in process mining, building software designed to gather data from people's interactions with business applications. It aims to uncover how organizations’ processes are actually performed, as opposed to how they were designed. For example, during a process mining project, pharma giant GSK discovered around 28,000 different variations for the process of running a sales order. Celonis was founded in 2011 and early customers included Siemens, with projects examining how processes run on the global engineering company’s SAP software. In 2021, SAP decided it wanted in on the same market and bought mining company Signavio, in part to help customers move from legacy software systems to the cloud. The ERP giant does not mandate Signavio for its migrations, but the software is bundled in packages under the moniker RISE with SAP, the lift-shift-and-transform commercial push SAP launched in 2021 to get users into the cloud and on its latest ERP offering, S/4HANA. The latest ruling is part of a set of legal disputes between Celonis and SAP. In March last year, Celonis filed a lawsuit in the US Court, Northern District of California, claiming the ERP giant had made it more difficult and expensive for third-party software companies to get hold of customer data stored in SAP's business software. In fact, the Munich court's decision represents only one of several ongoing disputes between SAP and Celonis, including patent actions brought by SAP in Germany and the United States. Celonis specializes in process mining, building software designed to gather data from people's interactions with business applications. For example, during a process mining project, pharma giant GSK discovered around 28,000 different variations for the process of running a sales order. Celonis was founded in 2011 and early customers included Siemens, with projects examining how processes run on the global engineering company’s SAP software. In 2021, SAP decided it wanted in on the same market and bought mining company Signavio, in part to help customers move from legacy software systems to the cloud. The ERP giant does not mandate Signavio for its migrations, but the software is bundled in packages under the moniker RISE with SAP, the lift-shift-and-transform commercial push SAP launched in 2021 to get users into the cloud and on its latest ERP offering, S/4HANA. Celonis was later allowed to amend and refile its complaint after the US court dismissed most of the claims. A trial is set for September 2027. SAP has also launched a case alleging a patent infringement action against Celonis at a Düsseldorf, Germany, court. It also filed suit in October last year at the District Court of Delaware over four US patents. Celonis has launched other cases alleging infringement by SAP, including in a Texas federal district court. ®

item.title: Review: Lanterns is a truly unique twist on the superhero genre
item.description: The trailers for HBO's DC Universe series Lanterns teased a show that eschewed the usual superhero hijinks in favor of a gritty realism more in the vein of True Detective or Slow Horses . Personally, I liked the change. My verdict: Ignore the review bombing ; it's wonderful. The season wrapped with an emotionally charged, almost elegiac finale that fully delivered on that initial promise. I've found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives . But Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre. (Spoilers below, but no major reveals.) There are two primary storylines. The first takes place in 2016 with a mass shooting at a local football game in Rushville, Nebraska. Current Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and his new trainee, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), get involved in the investigation, to the annoyance of Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald), who initially doesn't think the case has any extraterrestrial connection. She is soon proved wrong when the suspect (an alien) self-detonates. Hal's power ring controls the damage, but the mystery remains. Read full article Comments

item.title: Admin: 'I spent all weekend on my servers' after Microsoft breaks Exchange Server with October updates
item.description: Microsoft has acknowledged that the October 2026 Windows Server updates may be destabilizing Exchange Server. The problems are related to this list of Windows Server updates (see here) and Microsoft makes it clear they are not related to the October 2026 security updates for Exchange Server. The software giant says the bug can hit Exchange Servers running Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022, and 2025. The glitch might not be immediate and could impact Exchange Server OWA, which can throw up connection glitches or cause lengthy email queues, "with email crawling to a halt." Rebooting the server might make the problem go away temporarily, but a more permanent workaround is a registry edit. The destabilization issue could impact Exchange Server 2016, 2019, and the new Subscription Edition (SE), says the Windows maker. Microsoft strongly advised that customers should not uninstall the October 2026 Windows Server update and stated, "Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem." However, for those administrators who found their weekend swallowed by borked Exchange Servers, the registry edit is currently the only workaround. The cause of the issue is a default limit on the amount of memory used by Endpoint Mapper when handling Endpoint Lookup calls. In Microsoft's Release Health Dashboard for Windows Server 2025 (Server 2022, 2019, and 2016 are also affected), the Microsoft said: "For workloads such as Exchange Server, the default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls might not be sufficient under heavy load." Hence, the instruction to use a registry setting to increase the maximum. It added, "We are investigating this issue and will provide more information when it is available." Customers were understandably frustrated. On Microsoft's support page, one wrote, "We have had the problem like every 20h since Wednesday, when we installed the windows updates for October and the exchange su. Reboot only solution," before noting that the registry setting appeared to have improved things. Another fumed, "Also please release your updates tested and without problems. Without giving us the job to test for you. We're already paying for the software and you want to make tests with us?! I spent all weekend on my servers because of this." The issue is bad form on the part of Microsoft and appears to be the result of a poorly thought-through default applied in the operating system which impacted Exchange Server. Microsoft has yet to commit to issuing an out-of-band update to resolve the issue, after all, not every customer is affected, and the problem depends heavily on how busy a server is. However, at least there's a registry workaround that might do the trick while Microsoft ponders its next move. ®

The issue is bad form on the part of Microsoft and appears to be the result of a poorly thought-through default applied in the operating system which impacted Exchange Server. Microsoft has yet to commit to issuing an out-of-band update to resolve the issue, after all, not every customer is affected, and the problem depends heavily on how busy a server is. However, at least there's a registry workaround that might do the trick while Microsoft ponders its next move. ®

item.title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
item.description: Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift . For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced , and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro . But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front. That's right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement. Read full article Comments

item.title: Microsoft abandons UK AI supercomputer as grid struggles to keep up
item.description: Microsoft has reportedly pulled out of plans for Britain's largest AI supercomputer, because the government-backed project is facing the rather inconvenient problem of having no electricity to run it. The tech giant has terminated its agreement with British AI infrastructure startup Nscale for a planned datacenter in Loughton, Essex, according to The Telegraph, which first reported the withdrawal on Sunday. The decision follows reports that the site, which was supposed to begin operating in 2027, might not receive enough electricity from the grid until the early to mid-2030s. Microsoft was expected to be the anchor customer at Loughton, which Nscale had pitched as the UK's largest sovereign AI datacenter. Its departure leaves Nscale without a publicly announced customer for the site, although the neocloud insists the project is still going ahead. When the deal was announced in September 2025, the plan was to pack 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs into a 50MW facility, with room to expand to 90MW. Microsoft would use the computing power for its Azure cloud services, with the first chips expected in early 2027. One important detail remained: how to power it. As The Guardian reported last month, UK Power Networks warned Nscale that the grid capacity needed might not be available until the 2030s. A UK Power Networks spokesperson told The Register it could not discuss individual connections due to obligations under Section 105 of the Utilities Act. "However, in general, many datacenters, whilst they can connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the national transmission network which we do not own," the spokesperson said. Nscale, meanwhile, isn't letting the small matter of losing its biggest customer dampen its enthusiasm. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK. Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts,” Nscale told The Register. Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment. The project has already had its share of awkward moments. In March, it was revealed that the site earmarked for Britain's AI supercomputer was still being used as a scaffolding yard. Nscale has since cleared the land, but removing the scaffolding has proved easier than securing electricity. The government might be feeling a little red-faced too, having trumpeted the Loughton project as part of Microsoft's £22 billion UK investment announcement in September 2025. Just over a year later, Microsoft has walked away, and the site is still facing years of delays in getting the power it needs. The grid problems extend well beyond Essex. Ofgem proposed charging datacenter developers for connection requests earlier this year, hoping to discourage speculative projects from clogging up the queue. Demand for new connections had surged from 41GW to 12
item.content:encoded: Microsoft has reportedly pulled out of plans for Britain's largest AI supercomputer, because the government-backed project is facing the rather inconvenient problem of having no electricity to run it. The tech giant has terminated its agreement with British AI infrastructure startup Nscale for a planned datacenter in Loughton, Essex, according to The Telegraph, which first reported the withdrawal on Sunday. The decision follows reports that the site, which was supposed to begin operating in 2027, might not receive enough electricity from the grid until the early to mid-2030s. Microsoft was expected to be the anchor customer at Loughton, which Nscale had pitched as the UK's largest sovereign AI datacenter. Its departure leaves Nscale without a publicly announced customer for the site, although the neocloud insists the project is still going ahead. When the deal was announced in September 2025, the plan was to pack 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs into a 50MW facility, with room to expand to 90MW. Microsoft would use the computing power for its Azure cloud services, with the first chips expected in early 2027. One important detail remained: how to power it. As The Guardian reported last month, UK Power Networks warned Nscale that the grid capacity needed might not be available until the 2030s. A UK Power Networks spokesperson told The Register it could not discuss individual connections due to obligations under Section 105 of the Utilities Act. "However, in general, many datacenters, whilst they can connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the national transmission network which we do not own," the spokesperson said. Nscale, meanwhile, isn't letting the small matter of losing its biggest customer dampen its enthusiasm. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK. Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts,” Nscale told The Register. Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment. The project has already had its share of awkward moments. In March, it was revealed that the site earmarked for Britain's AI supercomputer was still being used as a scaffolding yard. Nscale has since cleared the land, but removing the scaffolding has proved easier than securing electricity. The government might be feeling a little red-faced too, having trumpeted the Loughton project as part of Microsoft's £22 billion UK investment announcement in September 2025. Just over a year later, Microsoft has walked away, and the site is still facing years of delays in getting the power it needs. The grid problems extend well beyond Essex. Ofgem proposed charging datacenter developers for connection requests earlier this year, hoping to discourage speculative projects from clogging up the queue. Demand for new connections had surged from 41GW to 125GW in less than a year, with datacenters accounting for at least 80GW. Some UK datacenter developers have turned to gas-powered generation rather than wait years for a grid connection, while others face growing resistance from the people living nearby. Residents near Google's Waltham Cross facility complained about noise, lighting and poor consultation at a public meeting in July. Britain isn’t alone in finding that the AI boom comes with substantial infrastructure demands. In the US, public enthusiasm for datacenters appears to be cooling, with concerns about electricity costs and environmental impacts increasingly souring attitudes towards new developments. For all the billions being thrown at AI infrastructure, the industry is discovering that building datacenters is the easy part. Getting them connected to the grid, and keeping the neighbors happy, is proving rather more difficult. ®

item.title: Broadcom Wi-Fi bug turns sweet 16, still lets strangers hijack your router
item.description: A 16-year-old security flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi software could let attackers hijack millions of routers without knowing the network password, even though the chipmaker reportedly knew about the problem since 2018. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the vulnerability, dubbed "WPSplinter," revealing two bugs in Broadcom's proprietary Wi-Fi implementation that date back to at least 2010. An attempted fix arrived eight years later, but Kaiser claims it didn't fully resolve the problem. The bugs lie in Broadcom's handling of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets users connect devices to a wireless network without manually entering a password. Kaiser found that specially crafted WPS messages could corrupt the router's memory, allowing someone within Wi-Fi range to run their own code on the device. They wouldn't need the Wi-Fi password, and the router's owner wouldn't have to do a thing. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against routers supplied by Belgian internet providers Proximus and Orange. In one attack against an ASKEY TCG3000 gateway, he ran code on the device, pulled its Wi-Fi password from memory, and sent it back over the air. He then used the stolen credentials to join the network. He also found the flaw in Netgear and Technicolor routers supplied by VOO. He estimates that around 850,000 Proximus gateways could be affected, along with 500,000 at VOO and 210,000 at Orange Belgium. That puts the potential total at 1.56 million routers in Belgium alone, although Kaiser admits the figures are rough estimates. However, the problem is unlikely to stop at the Belgian border. Broadcom's Wi-Fi technology is used by dozens of manufacturers across hundreds of products, meaning the number of affected devices worldwide could be considerably higher. According to Kaiser, the chipmaker knew about the vulnerability back in 2018 and released a partial fix without publicly disclosing the problem. It subsequently recommended that manufacturers move away from its proprietary implementation and use the open-source hostapd software instead. Owners of routers running Broadcom's older eCos-based chips, including the BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, are in a particularly grim position. Kaiser calls the flaw a "forever day," meaning those devices may never get a fix. Routers using Linux-based BCM3390, BCM65xx, and BCM68xx chips aren't necessarily off the hook either, unless their manufacturers switch to hostapd. That leaves some older routers with no obvious route to a fix, while others depend on their manufacturers updating software that may be years out of support. Kaiser first reported the vulnerabilities to Broadcom on July 18, followed by a second report on July 27, giving the company and affected vendors 90 days before public disclosure. item.content:encoded: A 16-year-old security flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi software could let attackers hijack millions of routers without knowing the network password, even though the chipmaker reportedly knew about the problem since 2018. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the vulnerability, dubbed "WPSplinter," revealing two bugs in Broadcom's proprietary Wi-Fi implementation that date back to at least 2010. An attempted fix arrived eight years later, but Kaiser claims it didn't fully resolve the problem. The bugs lie in Broadcom's handling of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets users connect devices to a wireless network without manually entering a password. Kaiser found that specially crafted WPS messages could corrupt the router's memory, allowing someone within Wi-Fi range to run their own code on the device. They wouldn't need the Wi-Fi password, and the router's owner wouldn't have to do a thing. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against routers supplied by Belgian internet providers Proximus and Orange. In one attack against an ASKEY TCG3000 gateway, he ran code on the device, pulled its Wi-Fi password from memory, and sent it back over the air. He then used the stolen credentials to join the network. He also found the flaw in Netgear and Technicolor routers supplied by VOO. He estimates that around 850,000 Proximus gateways could be affected, along with 500,000 at VOO and 210,000 at Orange Belgium. That puts the potential total at 1.56 million routers in Belgium alone, although Kaiser admits the figures are rough estimates. However, the problem is unlikely to stop at the Belgian border. Broadcom's Wi-Fi technology is used by dozens of manufacturers across hundreds of products, meaning the number of affected devices worldwide could be considerably higher. According to Kaiser, the chipmaker knew about the vulnerability back in 2018 and released a partial fix without publicly disclosing the problem. It subsequently recommended that manufacturers move away from its proprietary implementation and use the open-source hostapd software instead. Owners of routers running Broadcom's older eCos-based chips, including the BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, are in a particularly grim position. Kaiser calls the flaw a "forever day," meaning those devices may never get a fix. Routers using Linux-based BCM3390, BCM65xx, and BCM68xx chips aren't necessarily off the hook either, unless their manufacturers switch to hostapd. That leaves some older routers with no obvious route to a fix, while others depend on their manufacturers updating software that may be years out of support. Kaiser first reported the vulnerabilities to Broadcom on July 18, followed by a second report on July 27, giving the company and affected vendors 90 days before public disclosure. Broadcom responded on July 28 to say a patch was available and advised him to contact affected manufacturers directly. The following day, however, the company declined to assign a CVE identifier or provide him with a copy of the notification it said it had sent to manufacturers through its customer portal. Kaiser also contacted Proximus, attempted to reach Orange Belgium and VOO, and passed his findings to Belgium's national cybersecurity authorities. He subsequently opened a case with CERT/CC, which closed it on August 4 because Broadcom was itself a CVE Numbering Authority and had declined to register the vulnerability. By October 15, a day before his presentation, Kaiser said none of the affected devices he had identified had received a patch. Kaiser hasn't reported evidence of attacks in the wild, but the potential for mischief is considerable. Someone parked outside a home or office could potentially compromise a vulnerable router, steal network credentials, or use their access to interfere with traffic. Kaiser also credited AI with speeding up the investigation. He reckons the work would ordinarily have taken him months, but with the help of frontier models, he finished it in less than a week. ®

item.title: Stratospheric airship flew from US to Japan to test sky cell tower concept
item.description: Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey's length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky. The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock. “We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we're twice as high as air traffic and we're above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen , founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we're still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.” Read full article Comments

item.title: Original Voyager team member talks to us about the astonishing scientific info the 50-year-old probe gathered
item.description: It's been nearly half a century since the Voyager probes launched from Earth on a mission to explore the outer solar system, and they're still running. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or YouTube. You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live. You're probably familiar with some of Voyager's iconic images, like the Pale Blue Dot and and its portraits of the outer planets. Those photos and observations wouldn't have been possible without Voyager's imaging team, eight members of which were selected from scientists from around the world. The UK's sole representative, Dr. Garry Hunt, joins us on this episode of The Kettle to discuss his role in the Voyager program, the future of the mission, and the state of science in the UK, US, and beyond. I'm your host, Brandon Vigliarolo, and we have a very special episode for you this week. We're gonna step away from the doom and gloom of AI and the silliness of Silicon Valley to talk about something and to someone of considerably more historic importance. The Voyager space missions will mark fifty years of exploring the solar system and beyond next year. With us to talk about this is Reg Reporter Richard Speed and our very special guest, British astrophysicist Dr. Garry Hunt who was a member of the original Voyager imaging team. Thank you so much, Dr. Hunt, for coming on. And I'm gonna turn this over to Richard today, since you two have such a history together working on stories for The Reg, and I'm excited to hear about what he's going to pick your brain about. So Richard, take it away. Richard Speed (00:46) Well Dr. Hunt, we've spoken a lot about the Voyager project over the years, but for anyone who's not aware of it, I wonder if you could summarize the mission, which is, I know, a big ask, and also what your role in it is and was. Garry Hunt (01:00) Well indeed, it's a unique mission in the sense that every 176 years the major planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, line up virtually in a straight line. And we wanted to explore the outer planets 'cause we've never been there before. I'm talking in the 1970s, late 1960s, '70s. So this is an unknown world. We thought that the major planets were keys to understanding the origin of the solar system, indeed the origin of life, so sending space missions there was a priority. But it needed to be done in a very economical way. With the planets lined up, that meant we could get there in the quickest way, requiring less fuel, and it would be the best way of going about it. Thank you so much, Dr. Hunt, for coming on. And I'm gonna turn this over to Richard today, since you two have such a history together working on stories for The Reg, and I'm excited to hear about what he's going to pick your brain about. So Richard, take it away. Richard Speed (00:46) Well Dr. Hunt, we've spoken a lot about the Voyager project over the years, but for anyone who's not aware of it, I wonder if you could summarize the mission, which is, I know, a big ask, and also what your role in it is and was. Garry Hunt (01:00) Well indeed, it's a unique mission in the sense that every 176 years the major planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, line up virtually in a straight line. And we wanted to explore the outer planets 'cause we've never been there before. I'm talking in the 1970s, late 1960s, '70s. So this is an unknown world. We thought that the major planets were keys to understanding the origin of the solar system, indeed the origin of life, so sending space missions there was a priority. But it needed to be done in a very economical way. With the planets lined up, that meant we could get there in the quickest way, requiring less fuel, and it would be the best way of going about it. So the opportunity came and NASA funded a mission to send two spacecraft at this unique time, which was in the mid '70s, 1977, to the major planets. NASA sent out an invitation to tender. They selected the ten instruments. Imaging had as an instrument in concept had been suggested, but they wanted a team of real scientists, not astronomers, not basic astronomers. They understood this is a chance to do real detailed science, real physics, real chemistry, the whole understanding of what went on. So they were looking for an interdisciplinary group of people. They selected eight people from invitations and I gather there were about nearly a thousand people proposed and of those eight I was chosen. Brandon (02:43) Wow. Garry Hunt (02:44) So I decided I suddenly found myself in this incredible position. I'm there to represent atmospheric physics. I want to understand the physics, the meteorology of the major planets. So here is an opportunity to explore the outer planets to learn about why we wanted to go to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. However, funding was tight. The president at the time was Nixon, and we only had funding as far as Jupiter and Saturn. So we were treading new territory. At the time the mission was sort of decided, we had not been through the asteroid belt. So the first question was: would the spacecraft even get that far? And of course the pioneers had just been launched at the beginning of the '70s and they managed to get through and raised a lot of questions. So I was part of the imaging team, this amazing set of what I will call prima donnas, because we all were.
