item.content:encoded: KDE is marking its 30th birthday by showing X11 sessions the door. The newly released KDE Plasma 6.8 is Wayland-only, though X11 applications can still run through XWayland. The change arrives right on schedule after last month's beta. KWin handles both window management and display-server duties. That means X11-based screen-recording tools, for example, won't work any more. You can't "shade" windows – roll them up into the title bar and back – and that's not planned to come back. Restoring saved sessions can also behave differently. Applications cannot freely position their own windows under Wayland, leaving placement to the compositor. Saying that, there are lots of tweaks and refinements in this release. The Spectacle screenshot tool can now include system audio and microphone input in its screen recordings. Plasma 6.8 integrates with non-KDE tools better. For instance, KDE's browser integration now supports the Flatpak version of Microsoft's Edge browser. GTK2 applications also get better dark-theme matching. Internationalization is getting better – for example, the Clock understands the Bikram Sambat calendar, and Amharic is now supported in KDE's on-screen keyboard. The System Monitor app has better tracking of VRAM usage as well as main memory, and can pin tasks to certain CPU cores. There's better multi-monitor handling: screens are color-coded as well as by make and model, which is helpful if you have multiple identical monitors. There are more authentication options in KDE's VPN support too. The Union theming system is in beta, though not enabled by default. KWin can also apply matching effects to windows with client-side decorations, such as Valve's Steam client. Plasma's High Dynamic Range (HDR) support is better: it follows ICC color profiles, and understands Hybrid Log Gamma. On Nvidia GPUs, Plasma 6.8 enables triple-buffered output, resulting in smoother animations and transitions. Speaking of animations, more system effects – such as desktop "peek" and window "aperture" (when windows slide to the edge of the screen out of the way) – now respect the global animation settings. The Wayland-only session requires alternatives to remote-access tools that depend on an X11 desktop session, but the built-in Remote Desktop server, based on KRdp, has been improved. It's faster, it can adapt to slower connections on the fly, the clipboard is now bi-directional between host and remote system, and an exclusive mode can lock the host's screen while providing a virtual display sized to the client's window. KRdp uses Microsoft's Remote Desktop Protocol, but there's also Krfb if you prefer VNC instead. If you really need individual remote Wayland applications over SSH, then Waypipe is the way to go. The full changelog has all the details of the changes. Kubuntu 27.04 – recently announced as being codenamed "Tenacious T-Rex" – should include Plasma 6.8 when it arrives in April next year. KDE's internal metrics showed more than 95 percent of Plasma 6.6 users running Wayland in June. Including older versions, adoption was about 76 percent. Even so, we suspect that some users won't be happy with this change. With 6.8 out of the door, and on its way into fast-moving distros near you, the SonicDE project, which aims to continue development of the X11-capable KWin from Plasma 6.7, may start to pick up more interest. The KDE Project started with founder Matthias Ettrich's announcement on the de.comp.os.linux newsgroup on October 14, 1996. Before KDE, there were some commercial proprietary Unix desktop environments that were ported to Linux. For instance, Caldera OpenLinux 1.0 shipped with Visix's Looking Glass – you can see a tiny screenshot of it in the OpenLinux 1.1 announcement – but none ever went FOSS. Xfce is slightly older – as founder Olivier Fourdan described in this 2009 article: "I started the project in late 1996, before GNOME or gtk+ even existed." The XForms Common Environment was released first, but in those early days, what was then called XFce wasn't open source. It also started out as a recreation of CDE, which was finally open sourced in 2012. This makes it an early equivalent of NsCDE, which we compared with the real thing in 2022. In its early days, the Qt C++ toolkit that KDE chose caused problems, which led to the establishment of the KDE Free Qt Foundation in case something bad happened to its creators. Qt's licensing situation improved in 2000, when Qt 2.2 became available under both the GPL and QPL, resolving the GPL-compatibility concerns surrounding KDE's foundations. Even holdout Red Hat started bundling KDE. Thirty years on, KDE remains one of the great survivors of the free desktop. Long may it continue. ®

item.title: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics
item.description: The studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Where do you go after Mario? It’s a question the team at Ubisoft Paris found itself pondering three years ago after wrapping up work on the charming turn-based tactics adventure, Mario + Rabbids: Sparks of Hope , sequel to its unexpected crossover hit, Mario + Rabbids: Kingdom Battle. By melding a rather specialist genre with video gaming’s biggest household name, the developer introduced chin-stroking strategic play to a whole new audience. “ Having the opportunity to work with the Mario franchise was a privilege, and it’s still something I’m very proud of,” says level designer director, Julien Vial. “I still remember seeing the first prototype and being blown away by all the possibilities . ” Now, Ubisoft Paris has returned with a new project, but this time the studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Rainbow Six. Where Mario and Rabbids saw squishy creatures bounce harmlessly across levels as Mario encased foes in honey, Rainbow Six Tactics, a turn-based tactical spin-off from Rainbow Six Siege , sees balaclava-clad insurgents take shrapnel rounds to the chest. A seamless tonal shift, then. Continue reading...

item.title: Ready player one? Why the games arcade is having a rebirth
item.description: After years of sprawling ‘forever’ games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming? • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here There’s an important semi-nostalgic movement happening in games, and I’m excited about where it’s heading. But I don’t want to get ahead of myself here. Over the last five years, major publishers, obsessed with the success of “forever games” such as Fortnite, Minecraft and Roblox, have been throwing hundreds of millions of dollars into their own sprawling, endlessly updating, battle-pass-infested mega franchises – each designed to take all our time and money. The result has been astounding failures such as Concord , Mindseye and Tales of the Shire. Even the good games – Crimson Desert, Path of Exile 2, Blood of the Dawnwalker – are so bloated they have become the unyielding masters of our precious few hours of free time. Continue reading...

item.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era
item.description: The kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changer When beloved art is revisited and revised, a familiar cry is often heard: “You’re ruining my childhood!” But with Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time, there are also livelihoods at risk: specifically, the man running the shooting gallery in Castle Town. In the original 1998 version of the game, he’d rip off players as they funnelled rupees and fudged the then still novel analogue-stick aiming. But in 2026 we have more responsive frame rates and a motion-controlled slingshot that allows precision adjustments. His targets tumble on the first go, and with them his entire business model. Even in Hyrule, the death of the high street seems inevitable. Bad news for him but great news for Link, a child of the forest who, as in 1998, steps into a vast fantasy kingdom to vanquish a great evil, but now does so with a number of improvements. The boy can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies to zip across grassy plains. He has a manual jump, free-rotating camera, a scrolling inventory bar that replaces menu screen faff and, crucially, a fatter wallet for holding all those gems he fleeces from struggling shooting gallery owners. Yes, we are being asked to applaud features that have been the norm for decades elsewhere, but it’s undeniably striking to enter familiar territory with a hero who feels this different under the thumbs. Continue reading...

item.title: The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on | Peter Lewis
item.description: The tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets are banking on us giving in to their ‘inevitability doctrine’. But in Australia, and around the world, resistance is rising Of all the drivers of the populist wave, one of the most powerful is the sense of inevitability that surrounds what we are told is the march of progress. In presenting the future as a fait accompli, it poisons the civic well by dealing us out of the game. While the US clings on to its status as the oldest constitutional democracy, the unholy alliance between the tech overlords and the White House is creating its own AI reality untethered to the will of the people . Continue reading...

item.title: I’m a pediatrician. Loss of human connection is the biggest threat to kids, not AI | Megan Moreno
item.description: Amid worries about children’s relationship to tech, the solution is often spending more time talking openly with each other We have become obsessed with the idea that screens are destroying human connection. The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagers addicted to phones , a loneliness epidemic and the dangers of AI . The release of The Social Reckoning leads us to ask, “How bad were those guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “ How bad am I if I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings. Continue reading...

item.title: Apple AirPods 5 review: the best open-fit earbuds yet
item.description: Upgraded, cheaper AirPods have noise cancelling, sound and controls to rival many plugged-in buds but without tips Apple’s latest AirPods set a new standard for open-fit buds with upgraded noise cancelling that now rivals many plugged-in designs of the same price. The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors . Connectivity: Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, H2 chip Battery life: four or five hours with ANC (22 hours with case) Water resistance: IP57 (up to 1 metre for 30 minutes ) Earbud dimensions: 30.2 x 18.3 x 18.1mm Earbud weight: 4.3g each Charging case dimensions: 46.2 x 50.1 x 21.2mm Charging case weight: 32.3g/34.7g Case charging: USB-C or wireless (Qi or Watch) Continue reading...

item.title: OpenAI’s Jason Kwon gave even-toned, reassuring answers to the Australian government. Did … ChatGPT write this?
item.description: Kwon’s answers were provided in a helpful, quiet and calm manner, but his mea culpa left the audience not much the wiser Open AI’s Jason Kwon flew 15 hours from San Francisco to Sydney to give the company’s first in-person mea culpa after it admitted – in an unsigned email, to a public departmental inbox – that one of its AI agents had accessed a Services Australia website without authorisation and grabbed data related to Medicare. Kwon – polite, friendly, even-toned – got through a potentially dicey parliamentary committee hearing unscathed, promising to do better and pledging assistance to Australia. No missteps, no viral moments, just delivering his answers helpfully, in a quiet and calm manner, sympathising with the questioner and the point they were making. Continue reading...

item.title: Mac mini M6 review: truly mighty but now more pricey
item.description: Apple’s cheapest desktop computer is no longer a bargain but its newest, fastest chip makes it a pocket powerhouse Apple’s latest Mac mini brings real speed and power for far more than everyday tasks in a practically pocketable form you can fit almost anywhere. The impressive new desktop machine is the first to receive an update to Apple’s latest M6 chip while remaining smaller than a headphones box. It is the cheapest computer Apple sells with an M-series chip, but like every other memory-containing piece of electronics, it has been hit by RAMageddon , driving up the starting price to £899 (€1,049/$899/A$1,449) from the £599 or equivalent of its M4 predecessor. Continue reading...

item.title: Pixel 11 Pro Fold review: the foldable with the best triple camera

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices. Continue reading...
